notes.title: A Problem with Vulnerabilities
notes.core: • If I know how Caesar cipher or rail fence works I can decrypt it • Is knowledge of the algorithm a vulnerability? Algorithm – secret? Can you assume secrecy of the algorithm. How can you ensure knowing the algorithm doesn’t help? Ensure secrecy in the key only i.e. doesn’t matter if you know how it works, if you don’t have the key you can’t break it.

notes.title: Basic Solution
notes.core: • Secrecy should only be in the key! • Kerckhoff’s Principle “The security of a cryptosystem must not be dependent on the secrecy of the algorithm; it should only depend on the secrecy of the key.”

notes.title: DES – Data Encryption Standard
notes.core: • Each round does transposition, substitution and XOR of plaintext and sub-key. • Each 64-bit plaintext block undergoes 16 rounds of encryption individually. • A 56-bit cipher key is used to generate a different 48-bit sub-key, Ki, for Round i. Key length is actually 64-bit but every 8th bit is discarded to form 56-bit key. • The 56-bit key then undergoes 2 permutations and left circular shift -> 48-bit sub-key is selected. 56-bit cipher key DES is a symmetric-key block cipher published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).

notes.title: 3DES – Triple Data Encryption Standard
notes.core: • In 2002, networked computing power cracked the 56-bit key in < 24 hours. But there was inertia to replace DES -> 3DES (key length = 56 x 3 = 168 bits). • Encrypt the plaintext blocks using single DES with key K1. • Now decrypt the output of step 1 using single DES with key K2. • Finally, encrypt the output of step 2 using single DES with key K3. Triple DES operates in 3 steps: Encrypt-Decrypt- Encrypt (Ek1Dk2Ek3); Reverse -> Decrypt

notes.title: AES – Advanced Encryption Standard
notes.core: • From 2024, 3DES will be deprecated by NIST due to its limited 64-bit plaintext block size support. This makes it vulnerable to birthday attacks. • AES includes three block ciphers: AES-128, AES-192 and AES-256. • Each cipher encrypts and decrypts plaintext in blocks of 128 bits. Number of encryption rounds depend on key size. • Each round does transposition, substitution and XOR of plaintext and sub-key. AES can theoretically be cracked with quantum computing

notes.title: RSA Key Generation
notes.core: (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) • Pick two large distinct random primes (p and q) • Calculate n= pq • Calculate φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) (φ(n) – Euler’s totient function) • Pick e = number less than φ, co-prime to φ • Calculate d ➢d*e mod φ(n) = 1 • Public key is (e, n) • Private key is (d, n) • It is computationally infeasible to compute d from e and n alone. Only e and n are made known. Co-Primes: No common factor except 1 HCF/GCD = 1

notes.title: Birthday Attack Quantitative Basics
notes.core: In a group of 23 people, the probability that there are at least two persons on the same day in the same month is greater than 1/2 Proof. The probability that none of the 23 people has the same birthday Thus, 1 – 0.493 > 1/2 • The reason the birthday paradox works is that we are not just looking for matches between one fixed date and the other dates. We are looking for matches between any two dates in the set, so there are more opportunities for matches.

notes.title: What is considered Complex?
notes.core: • Complexity essentially measures how often neighbouring bits in a segment change value. • Assume there are 8 bytes in a segment (block): ➢Count the number of times the bits change value in each bytes. ➢Maximum value is 7, e.g. 10101010 or 01010101 • Do the same for each of the 8 bytes • The maximum number of changes is 2 x 8 x 7 = 112 (2:horizontal and vertical variations). • The complexity of a segment c = actual changes / 112 . • Define a threshold value T, which is a parameter of the algorithm. • If c > T then the segment is complex. No standard complexity threshold value, Typically, T is around 0.3

notes.title: Authorisation
notes.core: Already authenticated (proved you are who you claim to be), but are you authorised to carry out a particular action? Authorisation : What you are allowed to do Reference • Three main types of access control systems: Discretionary Access Control (DAC), Role Based Access Control (RBAC) and Mandatory Access Control (MAC). • Ensures that authenticated subject can only access objects using secure and pre-approved methods.

notes.title: Discretionary Access Control (DAC) – Assigns access rights based on rules
notes.core: specified by users (owner). Subjects can determine who has access to their objects. The DAC model uses access control lists (ACLs) and capability tables. The OS checks the tables to determine the type of access allowed. • Owner (User) created the object e.g. a file • Group is a defined group of specific users • Other (World) is anyone else Discretionary Access Control Microsoft ACL – Group and Individuals Linux ACL – Owner –Group-World

notes.title: Role-Based Access Control
notes.core: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) – also known as non-discretionary access control. System administrators assign rights based on organizational roles instead of individual user accounts within an organization. It allows the organization to address the principle of least privilege. This gives an individual only the access needed to do their job, since access is connected to their job Centrify and Solarwinds use the concept of groups. Each group has individual file permissions and each user is assigned to groups based on their work role. This requires the organization to constantly review the role definitions and have a process to modify roles to segregate duties. If not, role creep can occur. Role creep is when an individual is transferred to another job/group and their access from their previous job still stays with them.

notes.title: Mandatory Access Control
notes.core: Mandatory Access Control (MAC) – Access to resource objects is controlled by the OS based on system administrator-configured settings. MAC uses “security labels” to assign resource objects. Security labels have: classification (Top secret, Confidential, Unclassified, etc) and category/clearance levels (specific department or project – provides “need to know”). Each user account (subject) is also assigned classification and category properties. User access is granted if both properties match. MAC is the most secure access control but requires a considerable amount of planning and system management due to constant updating of objects and account labels. TOP SECRET SENSITIVE UNCLASSIFIED

notes.title: Principle of Least Privilege
notes.core: • The principle of least privilege (POLP) is a security best practice that requires limiting privileges to the minimum necessary to perform the job or task. • IT administrators often reference this principle when assigning access rights for user accounts, admin rights and configuring computer security settings. • Reduces the risk of un-authorized access to critical systems or sensitive data by compromising a low-level user account, device, or application.

notes.title: Principle of Least Privilege on Mobiles
notes.core: Mobile applications increasingly want access to various functions on your mobile device, such as your location and contacts book. A classic example of this is flashlight applications. These apps only turn the LED of the device on and off, so do not require access to phone information such as location, contacts, calls, or SMS messages. In a specific case related to this type of flashlight application, a banking Trojan that targeted Android users was installed and executed. The app requested device administrator permissions and also sought to steal the banking credentials of its victims. A mobile app may be considered intrusive or malicious due to the permissions it requests when it is installed, and the activities it then carries out. disguised

notes.title: Separation of Duties
notes.core: • Separation of duties (SoD), or segregation of duties, is a control mechanism in organizations that divides tasks and responsibilities for a process among multiple people • Prevents any single individual from having complete control over it, thus reducing the risk of fraud, errors, and security breaches. • For example, the person authorizing a paycheck should not also be the one who can prepare them.

notes.title: What is a (Computing) System?
notes.core: A computer system consists of hardware and system software that work together to run application programs. Specific implementations of systems change over time, but the underlying concepts do not. All computer systems have similar hardware and software components that perform similar functions. “Computer System: A Programmer’s Perspective” Randal E. Bryant & David R. O’Hallaron An integrated combination of hardware, software, computational tasks. It processes input, executes instructions, stores information, and produces output, often through an operating system that manages these functions. Computing systems can range from personal computers and smartphones to large cloud infrastructures and embedded devices. “Computer System” by ChatGPT

notes.title: (Computing) System Layers
notes.core: Architecture that distinguishes CPU, I/O devices, and main memory with the key characteristic is that memory holds both data and instructions. Von Neumann Computer Architecture Adversaries can attack a computer system without understanding these layers because the security vulnerabilities and their exploits often cross layer boundaries. So, the computer security specialists need to understand how complex software systems are executed.

notes.title: Hardware Attack
notes.core: A counterfeit attack involved the distribution of malicious or tampered hardware components that compromised the security of devices → hardware trojans with backdoors, compromised hardware during manufacturing, or dropping a USB to emulate keyboard keystrokes A Fault injection attack alters the device operation by physically tampering with hardware components → inject voltage/clock glitches to change the CPU instructions, or inject faults via periodic electromagnetic pulses A micro-architectural attack targets the implementation of a system’s microarchitecture → speculative attacks to read arbitrary memory, or exploiting vulnerabilities of DRAM for privilege escalation

notes.title: Hardware Attack Example: Spectre
notes.core: How is the data stored in memory? The variables x and y may be stored in registers. The variable x indexes array1, and the value stored in array1 indexes into array2, which stretches over multiple pages. Speculative execution attacks to read arbitrary memory via a timing side-channel attack to pass information from the microarchitectural layer to the software layer. Anything wrong with the code? Is the code harmless? Can we easily make it harmless?

notes.title: Hardware Attack Example: Spectre
notes.core: Spectre is exploiting a design problem in modern CPUs, and there is no easy fix for this hardware root cause, so a lot of work was spent in 2018 to harden systems. CPU memory caches are not accessible from outside of the CPU, but if the CPU instruction needs data from the main memory (i.e., slow memory), the CPU has to wait quite a while. Simply guess a value and continue execution speculatively, rollback if the wrong guess, and commit the speculative computation if the correct guess.

notes.title: Software Attack
notes.core: • A control flow attack diverts the intended control flow of a program to execute malicious code → Stack smashing attacks to execute malicious code, or return-oriented programming attacks to construct malicious code via function returns • A code injection attack is an attack on a system where input is passed to a program (the generator), which generates executable code to be executed by another program (the executor) • A command injection attack is a code injection attack where an attacker sends input to an application to modify commands passed to a interpreter injected by the attacker

notes.title: Hypervisor / Virtualization Manager
notes.core: A hypervisor is a piece of software, usually not very big in terms of compute or storage footprint, which makes server virtualization possible. It forms an abstraction layer between the server's hardware resources and the operating system or containers. There are different types of hypervisors with different hardware abstraction approaches. “Hypervisor” from Learning VMWare vSphere by Rebecca and Abhilash Baremetal Hypervisor Hosted Hypervisor OS-Level Hypervisor (Container)

notes.title: Hypervisor / Virtualization Attacks
notes.core: • A hyperjacking attack aims to replace a hypervisor with a malicious hypervisor by injecting a malicious hypervisor below/above or totally replacing the legitimate hypervisor → the presence of the malicious hypervisor is difficult to detect from the operating system. • A virtual machine escape attack is a program to allows interaction between the VM and the underlying hypervisor or host operating system by breaking the isolation provided by the hypervisor → can be found in many popular hypervisors (e.g., Xen, KVM, VMware, Hyper-V, VirtualBox) • A virtual machine rootkit attack installs a rootkit running underneath an operating system (A special case of a hyperjacking attack) → rootkit may launch and run malware in separate invisible virtual machines that are hard to detect.

notes.title: Operating System (OS) Attacks
notes.core: • A loadable kernel module attack uses loadable kernel modules (e.g., drivers, network protocols) to inject malicious code into an OS kernel → Malicious kernel modules have almost unlimited access to programs on monolithic kernels • A kernel rootkit attack is an attempt to install (persistently/volatilely) a rootkit within an OS kernel with or without privilege escalation attacks → Kernel rootkits are difficult to detect, and hence a complete re-installation is usually required • A kernel privilege escalation attack gains access to resources that are normally protected from a user because OS kernels usually execute at higher privilege levels and protect resources against access from less privileged processes → Some OS put application processes into restricted execution environments called jails, and kernel privilege escalation attacks may be used to escape from the jail (jailbreaking).

notes.title: OS Attack Example: Kernel Privilege Escalation
notes.core: Horizontal privilege escalation - attacker gains access to another user’s account at the same privilege level to access valuable assets or information, leading to a privilege escalation attack and privilege elevation. Vertical privilege escalation - attacker increases the privileges of a compromised account to gain higher-level access, such as administrative or root privileges. Vertical escalation is particularly dangerous as it may grant attackers complete control over the system.

notes.title: What is a Network?
notes.core: A network is a system of interconnected people, devices, or organizations that exchange information, resources, or services. This can range from a physical mesh of wires or roads to a group of people forming a social or professional network. Examples: computer network, social network, infrastructure network, and broadcasting network. AI-Generated Definition A computer network is a collection of autonomous computers interconnected by a single technology. Two computers are said to be interconnected if they can exchange information. The connection need not be via a copper wire; fiber optics, microwaves, infrared, or communication satellites. Networks come in many sizes, shapes, and forms. They are usually connected to make larger networks, with the Internet being the most well-known example of a network of networks. “Computer Networks” by Tanenbaum and Wetherall

notes.title: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS)
notes.core: • Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) detects attacks without needing traffic flow over it. • NIDS can be connected to a Hub network in promiscuous mode or to a Switch network via port mirroring (span port) to monitor multiple/different sub-networks. • NIDS can be extended via Host IDS (HIDS) or agents for a larger attack detection scope • Support deep packet inspection (DPI) – examines the packet’s header and data, to get more detailed than packet filtering • Use signature-based or statistical anomaly-based detection techniques with higher accuracy

notes.title: Intrusion Protection Systems (IPS)
notes.core: • A Network Intrusion Prevention System (NIPS) does what a NIDS does, plus automated responses to block the intrusions, protect against system hijacking and data theft (including changing firewall settings). • NIPS is usually located inline between the firewall and the protected network and thus requires greater logging capacity and ability to respond in real-time.

notes.title: Network Proxy
notes.core: • A proxy firewall, or application gateway, protects network resources by redirecting web requests at the application layer (no direct connections with external servers). • Scans incoming traffic for layer 7 protocols like FTP or HTTP, and also offers deep packet inspection of the incoming data packets for possible maliciousness. • Functioning at a high level in the OSI stack enables them to detect and address spoofing and other sophisticated attacks; • Examines the data for content that is not allowed; can limit applications supported by network. • Provides private or anonymous Internet access (hides IP address).

notes.title: Application Proxy
notes.core: Examples: Symantec Advanced Security and Gateway ProxySG • Have extensive logging capabilities due to the ability to examine the contents of the entire network packet rather than just addresses and ports. • It can also cache frequently accessed web pages to reduce network traffic – improved network performance. • May not be well-suited for real-time or high-bandwidth applications.
